extra.message: Insecure Deserialization via pickle.loads() on untrusted user-supplied data — Remote code execution on the server via crafted pickle payload — full system compromise, ability to read/write database, exfiltrate all borrower PII and financial data. [verified: Same as finding 1: `pickle.loads(raw)` at line 61 on attacker-controlled data (body or base64-decoded blob) enables arbitrary RCE via malicious pickle deserialization.]

Code Injection via eval() on user-supplied expression — Arbitrary Python code execution on the server, despite restricted builtins — full system compromise. [verified: Same as finding 3: `eval(expr, {"__builtins__": {}})` at line 71 is bypassable via `().__class__.__bases__[0].__subclasses__()` chains despite restricted builtins.]

Insecure Deserialization via pickle.loads() on untrusted data — Arbitrary code execution on the server with the privileges of the application process. [verified: Same as finding 1: `pickle.loads(raw)` at line 61 on untrusted input allows arbitrary code execution via crafted `__reduce__` payloads.]

Code Injection via eval() on user-supplied expression — Arbitrary Python code execution on the server, enabling full system compromise. [verified: Same as finding 3: `eval(expr, {"__builtins__": {}})` at line 72 does not prevent sandbox escape via object introspection, allowing arbitrary code execution.]

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) via Jinja2 template string concatenation — Remote code execution via Jinja2 SSTI — ability to read arbitrary files, access environment variables and secrets, execute system commands through template engine sandbox escapes. [verified: Same as finding 2: `Template("Result: " + fragment).render()` at line 114 concatenates user fragment into template source code, enabling full Jinja2 SSTI with sandbox escape.]

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) via Jinja2 with unsanitized user fragment — Remote code execution on the server, allowing an attacker to read environment variables (including SECRET_KEY and DATABASE_URL), access the filesystem, and execute arbitrary commands. [verified: User-controlled 'fragment' query param is concatenated directly into a Jinja2 Template string at line 113: `Template("Result: " + fragment).render()`. The fragment becomes template source code, enabling full SSTI with object traversal to `os.popen`.]

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) via Jinja2 with user-controlled fragment — Arbitrary code execution on the server, enabling full system compromise. [verified: Same as finding 2: `Template('Result: ' + fragment).render()` at line 114 concatenates user fragment into template source, enabling SSTI with Python object traversal.]

OS Command Injection via os.system() with user-supplied host parameter — Remote code execution on the server with the privileges of the application process, leading to full system compromise, data exfiltration, or lateral movement. [verified: User-supplied 'host' query param is concatenated directly into `os.system("ping -c 1 " + host)` at line 148 with zero sanitization. The _wrk_gate token check is the sole defense and uses a timing-vulnerable `!=` comparison, not input validation.]

Command Injection via os.system() with user-supplied host parameter — Remote code execution on the server — full system compromise, data exfiltration, lateral movement. [verified: Same as finding 0: user-supplied 'host' query param is concatenated directly into `os.system("ping -c 1 " + host)` at line 148 with zero sanitization, enabling shell metacharacter injection.]

Hardcoded weak default SECRET_KEY for JWT signing — Complete authentication bypass — an attacker can forge valid JWT session tokens for any user role (admin, underwriter) and access all protected functionality and all borrower data. [verified: SECRET_KEY defaults to the well-known string 'dev-only-change-me-for-local-runs' (line 16) with no startup validation guard; if the env var is absent in any deployment, an attacker can forge HS256-signed JWT tokens for any user role including admin, achieving complete authentication bypass.]

Hardcoded Default JWT Secret Key — Complete authentication bypass; attackers can forge JWTs for any user including admin, gaining full access to all protected endpoints and data. [verified: This is the same vulnerability as finding [0]: SECRET_KEY defaults to the publicly-known 'dev-only-change-me-for-local-runs' with no startup guard, enabling arbitrary JWT forgery for any user if the env var is unset at deployment.]

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via Jinja2 |safe filter on user input — Cross-site scripting — arbitrary JavaScript execution in the victim's browser context, enabling session theft, credential phishing, or DOM manipulation. [verified: Same as finding 6: `Template("{{ card|safe }}")` at line 84 with `|safe` filter on user input disables auto-escaping, enabling XSS via HTML/JS injection.]

Reflected XSS via Jinja2 |safe filter on user-supplied card parameter — Execution of arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser when they visit the crafted URL, enabling session theft, credential phishing, DOM manipulation, and actions performed as the victim. [verified: `Template("{{ card|safe }}").render(card=card)` at line 83 renders user-controlled 'card' query param through Jinja2's `|safe` filter, disabling HTML auto-escaping and allowing arbitrary HTML/JavaScript injection in the HTMLResponse.]

Reflected XSS via Jinja2 |safe Filter — Arbitrary JavaScript execution in the victim's browser context; session theft, credential phishing, and DOM manipulation. [verified: Same as finding 6: `Template("{{ card|safe }}").render(card=card)` at line 84 applies `|safe` to user input, disabling HTML escaping and allowing arbitrary script injection in the response.]

Permissive CORS reflecting arbitrary Origin header with credentials — Cross-origin data theft — any malicious website can make authenticated requests to the API with the victim's session cookies, reading sensitive borrower data and performing actions as the victim. [verified: Same as finding 7: reflected Origin with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` at line 100 creates universal CORS bypass for credentialed cross-origin requests.]

Permissive CORS with Credential Reflection — Cross-origin attacks where a malicious website can make authenticated requests to the API using the victim's session cookies, reading sensitive data and performing state-changing operations. [verified: Same as finding 7: Origin header echoed to ACAO at line 100 with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` creates universal credential-bearing CORS bypass.]

Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via Jinja2 |safe filter on user input — Arbitrary JavaScript execution in the victim's browser, enabling session hijacking, credential theft, and phishing. [verified: Same as finding 6: Jinja2 `|safe` filter at line 84 disables HTML escaping on user-supplied 'card' parameter, enabling arbitrary JavaScript injection in the HTML response.]

Path Traversal — arbitrary file write via user-controlled 'name' parameter — Arbitrary file write on the server filesystem — overwrite application code, configuration files, or plant malicious files leading to code execution. [verified: Same as finding 5: `BASE_EXPORT_DIR / name` at line 144 with `mkdir(parents=True)` and `write_bytes(body)` allows path traversal to write arbitrary files using `../` sequences.]

CORS Misconfiguration — Reflected Origin with Credentials — Cross-origin theft of authenticated API responses including PII, financial data, and internal notes. [verified: Same as finding 7: Origin header reflected to Access-Control-Allow-Origin at line 100 with credentials enabled allows any origin to make authenticated cross-origin requests.]

XML External Entity (XXE) Injection via lxml with DTD and entity resolution enabled — Arbitrary file read from the server filesystem (e.g., environment files, source code), SSRF to internal services, and potential denial of service via entity expansion. [verified: lxml parser at line 134 is configured with `load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, no_network=False` on untrusted POST body XML, enabling external entity definition for local file reads (e.g., `/etc/passwd`) and SSRF.]

XML External Entity (XXE) Injection via permissive lxml parser — Local file disclosure, internal network scanning via SSRF, denial of service via XML entity expansion. [verified: Same as finding 4: lxml parser at line 134 with `load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, no_network=False` on untrusted XML enables XXE for local file reads and SSRF.]

Path Traversal / Arbitrary File Write via user-controlled 'name' parameter — Arbitrary file write anywhere on the filesystem, enabling code execution (e.g., overwriting Python modules, cron jobs, or SSH authorized_keys) and data destruction. [verified: Same as finding 5: `BASE_EXPORT_DIR / name` at line 144 uses unsanitized user path enabling `../` traversal and arbitrary file write via `target.write_bytes(body)`.]

XXE Injection via lxml parser with DTD and entity resolution enabled — Arbitrary local file disclosure, server-side request forgery, and potential denial of service. [verified: Same as finding 4: lxml.etree.XMLParser at line 135 with `load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, no_network=False` on attacker POST XML enables XXE attacks.]

Missing rate limiting on authentication endpoints enables brute-force attacks — An attacker can brute-force user credentials by submitting unlimited login attempts without any throttling, lockout, or CAPTCHA challenge. Combined with the known demo accounts and weak default passwords, this allows unauthorized account access. [verified: Same as idx 2/6 — no rate-limiting middleware, per-route throttling, or failed-attempt tracking exists on any auth endpoint; the only mitigation is PBKDF2 cost, which does not prevent automated brute-force against weak passwords.]

Missing rate limiting on all authentication endpoints — Attackers can perform unlimited brute-force password attacks against user accounts, enumerate valid credentials, flood the system with registrations causing resource exhaustion, and attempt large-scale credential stuffing without throttling. [verified: No rate-limiting middleware, decorator, per-IP tracking, or account lockout exists anywhere in the codebase on POST /api/auth/login (line ~651), register (line ~624), password-reset/request (line ~683), or password-reset/confirm, allowing unlimited brute-force credential attacks.]

Missing rate limiting on authentication endpoints (login, register, password-reset) — Credential brute-forcing, account enumeration via timing, denial of service against auth endpoints. [verified: Same as idx 2 — the login, register, and password-reset endpoints have zero rate limiting, throttling, or brute-force protection anywhere in the application, enabling unlimited credential stuffing and password guessing.]

Sensitive password reset token written to plaintext log file — Account takeover — an attacker with filesystem access (or via path traversal) can read active password reset tokens and reset any user's password. [verified: Line 688 writes the raw (unhashed) password reset token to a local log file via mock_log('email.log', {..., 'reset_token': raw_token}); the token is stored before hashing and is the active credential needed to consume the reset, enabling account takeover by anyone with filesystem read access.]

Password reset tokens written in plaintext to local log file — Account takeover — anyone with filesystem access can read the log, extract reset tokens, and reset passwords for any user. [verified: Same finding as idx 1 — line 688 logs the raw password reset token to storage/mock_logs/email.log in plaintext before hashing; no sanitization or redaction is applied, enabling token extraction and account takeover via filesystem read.]

Timing Attack on Internal Operations Token Gate (String != Comparison) — An attacker who can measure response-time differences across many requests can brute-force the INTERNAL_OPS_TOKEN character by character, gaining access to the /ops router which exposes command injection, code execution (eval), pickle deserialization, SSTI, XXE, path traversal, and SSRF endpoints. [verified: The `_wrk_gate` dependency at line 19 uses Python's `!=` operator for comparing `x-internal-token` against `INTERNAL_OPS_TOKEN`, which short-circuits on first mismatched byte and leaks timing information; `hmac.compare_digest` is already used elsewhere in the codebase (security.py:40, main.py:1680) for constant-time comparison.]

Log injection via unsanitized user input written to application logs — An attacker can inject forged log entries, manipulate log-based monitoring and alerting, obscure their real actions, or inject control characters that disrupt log parsing tools. [verified: `logger.warning("underwriting intake body=%s auth=%s", wire_text, request.headers.get("authorization"))` at line 32 logs unsanitized request body and the Authorization header in plaintext, enabling both log injection (newline forging) and credential exposure to anyone with log access.]

Sensitive data exposure — Authorization header logged in plaintext — Credential leakage via logs — if an attacker gains read access to application log files (or the logs are shipped to a SIEM with broad access), they can harvest valid JWT tokens or API keys contained in logged Authorization headers. [verified: Same as finding 8: `logger.warning()` at line 33 logs the Authorization header in plaintext and unsanitized body text, enabling credential exposure and log injection attacks.]

Open Redirect via user-controlled 'lane' query parameter — Phishing and social engineering — attacker can craft URLs that appear legitimate (starting with the trusted domain) but redirect victims to attacker-controlled sites to steal credentials. [verified: Same as finding 11: `RedirectResponse(lane)` at line 39 with unvalidated user-controlled redirect target enables phishing via open redirect.]

Sensitive Data Exposure — Authorization Token Logged in Plaintext + Log Injection — Credential leakage to anyone with log access; log forgery can mislead incident response and auditing. [verified: Same as finding 8: Authorization header logged in plaintext at line 33 via `logger.warning()` exposes credentials; unsanitized body text enables log forgery via newline injection.]

Open Redirect via user-controlled 'lane' parameter — Phishing and credential theft by redirecting authenticated users to malicious sites that appear legitimate. [verified: Same as finding 11: `RedirectResponse(lane)` at line 39 with no URL validation enables open redirect to attacker-controlled phishing sites.]

Mass assignment via unsanitized dict merge from user JSON payload — An attacker can override security-relevant fields (role, tier, approved status) in the workset, potentially elevating their privileges or bypassing authorization checks that consume this workset data. [verified: `workset.update(payload)` at line 66 merges attacker-supplied JSON into the workset dict with no field allowlist, allowing override of `role`, `tier`, `approved`, and `balance` keys to arbitrary values.]

Account/handle enumeration via distinct error responses in verifier check — Handle enumeration — attacker discovers which handles exist, then brute-forces the weak 4-digit verifier on valid handles. [verified: The `/ops/identity` endpoint at line 94 returns 404 for unknown handles and 403 for wrong verifiers — distinct status codes and messages enable handle enumeration, after which the 4-digit numeric verifier is brute-forceable.]

Weak pseudorandom number generator used for nonce generation — Predictable nonce generation — an attacker who observes multiple nonce outputs can reconstruct the PRNG state and predict future nonces, potentially undermining any security mechanism that relies on the nonce's unpredictability. [verified: Same as finding 9: `random.choice()` at line 129 uses weak Mersenne Twister PRNG instead of `secrets.choice()` for nonce generation; outputs become predictable with sufficient observation.]

Privilege elevation via forgeable badge cookie/header check — An attacker who knows the internal ops token can also send a forged x-ops-badge header or ops_badge cookie with value 'lead' to gain elevated operational privileges within the /ops subsystem. [verified: The `ops_badge` cookie or `x-ops-badge` header is checked via `badge == "lead"` at line 140 with no cryptographic verification; anyone who knows the internal ops token can also forge this header/cookie to gain elevated lane/payroll/casework privileges.]

Use of Cryptographically Weak PRNG for Token Generation — Predictable tokens enable session hijacking, password reset token guessing, and bypass of randomness-based security controls. [verified: Same as finding 9: `random.choice()` at line 129 uses cryptographically weak Mersenne Twister PRNG for nonce generation instead of the `secrets` module.]

Account enumeration via distinct error response at user registration — An attacker can build a list of valid user emails on the platform, which can then be targeted for credential stuffing, phishing, or password-reset attacks. [verified: The register endpoint at line 627-628 returns HTTP 409 with 'Email is already registered' for existing emails vs 200 for new registrations, creating a distinct, attacker-observable response that leaks account existence with no uniform-response control.]

User enumeration via registration endpoint (409 on existing email) — Account enumeration — attacker can build a list of registered email addresses for targeted phishing, credential stuffing, or password spraying attacks. [verified: Same as idx 0 — the register endpoint at line 627-628 returns HTTP 409 for duplicate emails vs 200 for successful registration with no uniform-response control, enabling email enumeration.]

Missing authorization: support specialist can edit any loan application — A support specialist can modify any borrower's loan application terms, requested amounts, product selection, and financial data, potentially enabling loan fraud or disruption of underwriting workflows. [verified: Same as idx 13 — update_application allows support_specialist to mutate application fields and borrower profile data through lines 915-926 because the role check at line 914 only excludes underwriters, while delete_application at line 940 correctly excludes both underwriter and support_specialist.]

Privilege escalation — support specialist can mass-assign borrower profile fields via application update — Horizontal privilege escalation — a support_specialist can modify any borrower's personal information (name, email, phone), contact details, and financial data (revenue, years in business) through the application update endpoint, violating the principle of least privilege. [verified: update_application at line 914 blocks underwriters but lets support_specialist fall through to the mutation code at lines 925-926 where apply_profile_update mass-assigns PII/financial fields via setattr; delete_application at line 940 confirms the intended restriction by explicitly blocking support_specialist.]

Unvalidated file upload trusting client-controlled Content-Type — Attackers can upload files with dangerous content by spoofing the Content-Type header, enabling malware distribution through the document download endpoint. [verified: File type validation at line 1038 trusts the client-supplied Content-Type header (upload.content_type) against ALLOWED_CONTENT_TYPES with no server-side magic-bytes inspection; the spoofed content_type is stored and served as the download media_type at line 1085, enabling malicious file distribution.]

Business Logic Bypass — Missing Final-Status Guard Allows Overriding Terminal Decisions on Approved/Rejected Applications — An assigned underwriter or admin can retroactively change an already-approved application to rejected (or an already-rejected application to approved), defeating the intended finality of terminal statuses. This corrupts the application lifecycle, creates conflicting decision records, and undermines audit integrity. [verified: create_decision at line 1185 checks application.status against {'draft', 'withdrawn'} but omits FINAL_STATUSES {'approved', 'rejected'} defined at line 77, allowing an assigned underwriter or admin to overwrite a terminal application status with a new decision, contradicting the intended finality enforced in withdraw_application at line 969.]

CSV formula injection in admin data exports — If an admin opens an exported CSV containing malicious formula cells (crafted via borrower-controlled text fields), the spreadsheet application may execute commands, exfiltrate data, or install malware on the admin's machine. [verified: The csv_response helper at line 1490 uses csv.DictWriter.writerows() without stripping or prefixing formula-trigger characters (=, +, -, @) from borrower-controlled fields like business_name and purpose, enabling formula execution when an admin opens the exported CSV in a spreadsheet application.]

CSV Formula Injection in exported decisions spreadsheet — Client-side code execution on the admin's machine when opening the exported CSV in a spreadsheet application. [verified: export_decisions at line ~1536 passes rows containing user-supplied reasons and borrower_summary fields directly to csv_response without formula sanitization, enabling CSV formula injection when opened in a spreadsheet.]

Session cookie missing Secure flag by default — Session hijacking via MITM — network attackers can steal JWT tokens and impersonate users. [verified: set_session_cookie defaults COOKIE_SECURE to false (line 58), transmitting the JWT session cookie without the Secure flag; while HttpOnly and SameSite=lax are set, a MITM attacker on unencrypted HTTP can still capture the token. No compensating control forces Secure=true in production.]

Hardcoded database credentials in default DATABASE_URL — Direct, authenticated access to the PostgreSQL database by anyone who can reach the database port, enabling full data exfiltration, modification, or destruction of all loan applications, user PII, and financial data. [verified: The os.getenv fallback on lines 13-15 hardcodes postgres:postgres@localhost:5432/loan_portal; docker-compose.yml exposes port 5432 with identical credentials and .env.example prescribes the same, forming a complete stack with known defaults if DATABASE_URL is unset.]

Internal path disclosure via error response in /ops/pulse endpoint — Information disclosure — an attacker learns the server's internal directory structure (PRIVATE_EXPORT_DIR path), aiding in path traversal or other filesystem-based attacks. [verified: Same as finding 25: the error response at line 30 returns `str(exc)` and `exc.__class__.__name__` including `BASE_EXPORT_DIR` path and user-controlled `lot_ref`, disclosing internal filesystem paths.]

Reflected cookie from query parameter without security flags — Cookie injection — an attacker can set arbitrary cookie values through crafted URLs; if any application logic trusts this cookie, it could enable session manipulation or client-side attacks. [verified: `response.set_cookie("portal_crumb", marker)` at line 79 sets a cookie from user-controlled query param without HttpOnly, Secure, or SameSite flags; the cookie is not used elsewhere in the codebase so impact is limited, but it reflects unsanitized input into a cookie without security protections.]

Security headers disabled — X-XSS-Protection and CSP — Weakened browser security — disabling CSP and XSS filter removes defense-in-depth protections, making XSS exploitation easier if another injection vulnerability exists in the application. [verified: Same as finding 24: `X-XSS-Protection: 0` and `Content-Security-Policy: ''` at line 108 explicitly disable browser XSS defenses on a reachable endpoint with no compensating global security headers middleware.]

Security headers disabled — CSP and XSS-Protection turned off — Reduced browser security posture — XSS attacks become easier to exploit against users loading this endpoint. [verified: The `/ops/frame` endpoint at line 108 explicitly sets `X-XSS-Protection: 0` and `Content-Security-Policy: ''`, disabling browser XSS auditor and CSP protections on a reachable endpoint with no compensating global header middleware.]

Missing CSRF Protection on State-Changing Endpoints — Authenticated state-changing actions (like creating decisions, updating applications, deleting resources) can be triggered without user consent via same-site CSRF attacks. [verified: No CSRF token verification, double-submit cookie pattern, or custom header requirement exists on any state-changing route; authentication relies solely on HttpOnly SameSite=Lax cookies, which block cross-origin but not same-site form-driven CSRF when an XSS or open redirect coexists on the origin.]
